title: Adapting to the New Terrorism Landscape 25 Years After 9/11
gist: Twenty-five years after 9/11, the dominant U.S. terrorism threat is the unaffiliated American lone actor whose motives blend multiple ideologies and who emerges from online communities bound by resentment rather than politics. The shift is itself evidence that post-9/11 counterterrorism worked: attacks are far less lethal but far harder to detect, which argues for behavioral threat assessment over ideological classification.

themes.theme: Counterterrorism success created the current threat

insights.claim: Lone actors now dominate the U.S. terrorism landscape largely because the post-9/11 counterterrorism apparatus, including DHS, the National Counterterrorism Center, expanded surveillance and overseas operations, succeeded in making foreign-organized attacks far harder.
insights.so_what: Reframes a seemingly worsening threat picture as a measure of prior success, which matters for how counterterrorism budgets get argued.
insights.quote: Today, lone actors dominate the terrorism landscape in large part because the counterterrorism apparatus stood up after 9/11 was successful.
insights.locator: After 9/11, the U.S. government massively expanded
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: The internet accelerated the shift to lone actors by giving individuals access to propaganda, tactical guidance, and new communities and audiences without requiring membership in any formal group.
insights.so_what: Puts online platforms rather than foreign organizations at the center of the detection problem, with implications for content policy and platform liability.
insights.locator: The emergence of the internet also likely accelerated
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Lone actors lack formal training and support, making them less destructive than organized groups, but that same absence of organizational connections makes them far harder to identify before an attack.
insights.so_what: A structural trade-off: lower casualty tails but higher event frequency and lower predictability, which changes how risk should be modeled.
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: The most lethal jihadist attack in nearly a decade, the New Year's Day 2025 New Orleans Bourbon Street car ramming by Shamsud-Din Jabbar that killed 14 after he pledged allegiance to the Islamic State, illustrates how isolated radicalization simultaneously hid the plot and limited the damage.
insights.so_what: A concrete benchmark for the lethality ceiling of the current threat model, useful for calibrating event severity expectations.
insights.locator: The most lethal jihadist attack in nearly the last decade
insights.speaker: CSIS

themes.theme: Ideology is losing its diagnostic value

insights.claim: Without group doctrine, many perpetrators assemble motives from multiple traditions, as with Mauricio Garcia, who recorded white supremacist, neo-Nazi, misogynist and incel grievances plus admiration for other mass shooters before killing eight at a shopping mall in 2023.
insights.so_what: Ideological labels used by agencies and media increasingly fail to describe actual cases, undermining threat categorization.
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Patrick Crusius, who killed 23 people at an El Paso Walmart in 2019, combined white nationalist opposition to immigration with warnings about ecological collapse and denunciations of corporate power in his manifesto.
insights.so_what: Evidence that ideological blending is not new in 2026 but has been visible for years, so the classification problem is structural.
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Some attacks now sit at the edge of what counts as terrorism, mixing political iconography with nonpolitical motives such as humiliation, notoriety-seeking and admiration for earlier killers, as when Robin Westman killed 2 children and wounded 27 at a Minneapolis Catholic church in August 2025 while calling the plan art and displaying weapons marked with the phrase there is no message.
insights.so_what: Definitional ambiguity complicates official terrorism statistics and any dataset an analyst relies on for trend work.
insights.quote: displayed weapons covered with political memes, slurs, earlier killers’ names, and the phrase “there is no message.”
insights.locator: In August 2025, 23-year-old former student Robin Westman
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Scholars are actively split on whether ideology still explains lone actor terrorism, with some calling for new frameworks as ideological boundaries dissolve and others arguing the phenomenon only looks incoherent because analysts lack the right categories.
insights.so_what: Signals that the analytical consensus is unsettled, so confident ideological attribution after any given attack should be discounted.
insights.locator: These attacks and others like them have produced an active debate
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Perpetrators of U.S. terrorism and mass violence are almost always American men acting alone or with one or two others, many escalating amid acute personal crisis such as mental illness episodes and social isolation.
insights.so_what: A stable demographic and situational profile that is more actionable for prevention than ideology.
insights.locator: Perpetrators of terrorism and other mass violence
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Most attackers display warning signs beforehand, confiding in family or friends, posting plans and grievances online, or unsettling those around them, and most must obtain a weapon, typically a firearm.
insights.so_what: Identifies the specific intervention points, which is where prevention spending and platform reporting tools should concentrate.
insights.locator: Perpetrators of terrorism and other mass violence
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: Prevention should shift toward clearer reporting channels, better behavioral threat assessments and more accessible crisis services, with a more ambitious upstream agenda covering mental health access for men, family and student support, firearm safeguards for at-risk individuals, and online mechanisms that make threats easier to report.
insights.so_what: The policy direction that would follow from the analysis, relevant to behavioral health and threat-assessment service providers.
insights.locator: Prevention therefore requires clearer reporting channels
insights.speaker: CSIS

insights.claim: The United States should preserve the post-9/11 capabilities that make another large organized attack far harder while accepting that those same tools cannot address the diffuse lone actor threat.
insights.so_what: Argues for additive, not substitutive, counterterrorism spending, which implies budget growth rather than reallocation.
insights.speaker: CSIS
